name: VEXAS syndrome
aliases: Vacuoles, E1 enzyme, X-linked, Autoinflammatory, Somatic syndrome

reference.source: Firestein & Kelley's Textbook of Rheumatology / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Almost exclusively affects men over 50 years, reflecting an acquired somatic mutation on the X chromosome
Presents as treatment-refractory systemic inflammation with recurrent fevers, neutrophilic dermatosis, chondritis of the ears or nose, and inflammatory ocular disease
Frequently overlaps clinically with relapsing polychondritis, Sweet syndrome, polyarteritis nodosa, or giant cell arteritis, but responds poorly to conventional treatment
Macrocytic anaemia and progressive cytopenias are near-universal, and there is a strong association with myelodysplastic syndrome and plasma cell dyscrasias
Characteristic cytoplasmic vacuoles are seen in myeloid and erythroid precursors on bone marrow aspirate
Diagnosis is confirmed by demonstrating a somatic UBA1 mutation (typically affecting methionine-41) in haematopoietic cells
Venous and arterial thromboembolism is common and adds substantially to morbidity
Inflammation is often corticosteroid-dependent, with high relapse rates on tapering
reference.pathophysiology: VEXAS syndrome arises from an acquired somatic mutation in the UBA1 gene within haematopoietic stem cells. UBA1 encodes the principal E1 enzyme that initiates cellular ubiquitylation. The mutation, usually at the p.Met41 site, impairs production of the cytoplasmic UBA1 isoform, disrupting ubiquitin-dependent protein turnover and triggering unchecked activation of innate immune and inflammatory pathways. The affected clone expands within the myeloid lineage, producing the diagnostic cytoplasmic vacuoles in myeloid and erythroid precursors and driving both the systemic autoinflammatory phenotype and a predisposition to myelodysplasia.
additionalDifferentials: Polyarteritis nodosa and other systemic vasculitides
additionalInvestigations: Targeted or next-generation sequencing of UBA1 in peripheral blood or bone marrow to detect the somatic mutation
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine looking for cytoplasmic vacuoles in myeloid/erythroid precursors and features of myelodysplasia
Full blood count and blood film demonstrating macrocytic anaemia and evolving cytopenias
Inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP, ferritin) which are typically markedly elevated
Skin or cartilage biopsy showing neutrophilic infiltration or chondritis
Cross-sectional imaging and vascular studies to assess thromboembolism and organ involvement
redFlags: Progressive cytopenias or transfusion dependence signalling evolution to myelodysplastic syndrome
Refractory systemic inflammation despite escalating immunosuppression
Weight loss and constitutional decline suggesting an underlying haematological malignancy
reference.prognosis: VEXAS syndrome is a serious, progressive disorder with substantial mortality driven by uncontrolled inflammation, thromboembolism, and haematological progression to myelodysplasia. Many patients remain corticosteroid-dependent; allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the only potentially curative option, while hypomethylating agents such as azacitidine and JAK inhibition are used to control disease.
pitfalls: Attributing refractory relapsing polychondritis or Sweet syndrome in an older man to the classic diagnosis alone and missing the underlying UBA1 clone
Overlooking macrocytosis and early cytopenias as clues to a marrow-based process
Failing to send UBA1 sequencing because the phenotype mimics a well-known rheumatological disease
Under-recognising the high thrombotic risk and not considering prophylaxis
Escalating immunosuppression without haematology involvement despite marrow dysplasia
management: Corticosteroids to control systemic autoinflammation, though most patients become corticosteroid-dependent
Steroid-sparing agents such as JAK inhibitors including ruxolitinib or IL-6 inhibition with tocilizumab, and azacitidine where there is associated myelodysplasia
Allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation as the only potentially curative option in suitable patients
Supportive care with red cell transfusion for macrocytic anaemia and thromboprophylaxis given the high venous thromboembolic risk
Regular monitoring of the full blood count and bone marrow for evolving cytopenias and progression to myelodysplastic syndrome
Prompt treatment of acute inflammatory flares and thromboembolic complications
Coordinated rheumatology and haematology care given the overlap of autoinflammation with clonal marrow disease
